First, Henry VIII married Anne Boleyn in 1533 after breaking with Rome to divorce his first wife, Catherine of Aragon. The Pope refused to recognise this divorce, meaning devout Catholics believed Catherine was still Henry’s lawful wife when Elizabeth was born. In 1536 Henry executed Anne Boleyn and passed an Act declaring Elizabeth illegitimate.

Second, the succession worried politicians when twenty-five-year-old Elizabeth became queen in November 1558. She was unmarried and had no Protestant child to inherit the throne if she died suddenly from illness. Consequently, her Privy Councillors and MPs in Parliament immediately urged her to choose either an English nobleman or a foreign prince as a husband.

London and the south-east contained many Protestants, whereas northern and western parishes still preferred Catholic Latin Mass, and Marian bishops sat in the House of Lords. In May 1559 Elizabeth passed the Act of Supremacy as Supreme Governor and the Act of Uniformity with a new Prayer Book and twelve-pence fines.

Around a third of English nobles and gentry, especially powerful families in the north of England like the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland, disliked Protestantism. tier_8m.text:
Sheep farming and enclosure caused serious rural poverty during Elizabeth's reign. Because English wool was very profitable to export, wealthy landowners fenced off open village fields and common land with hedges so they could keep large flocks of sheep instead of growing arable crops. Looking after sheep needed far fewer farm labourers than ploughing and harvesting grain, and landlords also raised rents sharply through rack-renting, which evicted tenant families onto the roads.

At the same time, England's population grew rapidly from around three million to nearly four million people by 1588. Having far more people meant there were not enough jobs, houses, or food supplies to go around, so bread prices rose steeply and landless young men wandered towards towns like London. Overall, I agree that economic pressures were the main reason because enclosure directly took away farm workers' jobs.

During his 1577–80 circumnavigation aboard the Golden Hind, Francis Drake sailed through the Strait of Magellan into the Pacific Ocean and raided unguarded Spanish ports like Valparaiso. tier_8m.text:
Sir Walter Raleigh played a vital role in organising the attempted colonisation of Virginia after Queen Elizabeth granted him a six-year royal patent in March 1584. Although Elizabeth forbade her favourite courtier from sailing in person, Raleigh sent Amadas and Barlowe on a scouting voyage in 1584, named the territory Virginia in the Queen's honour, brought Manteo and Wanchese to London, and raised £40,000 from investors to equip the 1585 expedition.

Rivalry with Catholic Spain also drove English colonisation plans in the mid-1580s. As relations with Philip II worsened toward open war in 1585, English leaders wanted a North American base near the Caribbean so privateers could attack Spanish treasure ships and challenge Spain's New World empire. Overall, I disagree that trade was the main reason because rivalry with Spain and Raleigh's ambition mattered much more.
